name: Climate Images and Feelings: Affective Environmental Images
description:
How do pictures of climate change consequences, and of their positive counterparts, make people feel? This template rebuilds the norming study of Asutay (2026), "A balanced set of standardized affective environmental images for climate change research", Frontiers in Psychology 17:1944740. 587 Prolific participants rated 203 images from six domains (forests and wildfires, oceans, urban air quality, extreme weather, food and water, indigenous and rural communities), each with matched negative and positive pictures. Pleasantness of the set centred on neutral with a wide spread, pleasantness and activation were quadratically related, and people with higher perceived climate risk and stronger biospheric values reacted more strongly to the negative images; biospheric values also predicted more pleasant, more activating reactions to the positive images.

Participants give age and gender and answer an attention check. They then rate 30 images drawn at random (15 positive, 15 negative) in random order. For each image: "How does this image make you feel?" on pleasantness (1 unpleasant, 5 neutral, 9 pleasant) and activation (1 sleepy, 9 awake), then, on a second screen with the same image, "How relevant do you think this image is to climate change?" (1 not at all to 5 very much). Afterwards: belief in human-caused climate change (4 options), perceived risk of climate change to oneself, other people and non-human life (0–100 sliders), and the 16 values of the E-SVS (Steg et al. 2014) from −1 (against my principles) to 7 (of supreme importance).

Data: feel and relevance (imageslidergroup, keyed by image file name, matching imageInfo in the author's OSF data); risk (custom: self, others, nonhuman); values (matrix: hed1–3, ego1–5, alt1–4, bio1–4). Analysis: per-image means of pleasantness, activation and relevance; positive vs negative images by domain; linear mixed model of pleasantness and activation on image valence × biospheric values and image valence × perceived risk, with random intercepts for participants and images.

Stimuli: the author's images from OSF wup5m (selected from pexels.com, unsplash.com and the climate image sets of Lehman et al. 2019 and Ottavi et al. 2021), resized to 1024 px. They are used here with credit to the author and will be removed if the author objects.

Differences from the original study: (1) 197 images: 196 of the 203 rated images plus bio_pos_pic247, which was in the set but never shown in the original; 7 rated images are not in the OSF folder (2 positive ocean, 2 positive weather and 3 forest/wildfire images), so some domains are slightly unbalanced; (2) the attention check wording is not given in the paper and is a generic "select Three" item; (3) the E-SVS item wording follows Steg et al. (2014), since the paper does not print it; (4) SP-Survey layout instead of Qualtrics, with the activation end labelled "Awake" as in the paper's survey screenshot.
author: Asutay

elements.name: consent
elements.title: I agree to take part. Participation is voluntary and my answers are recorded anonymously for research.

elements.name: attention_check
elements.title: Attention check: please select the option “Three”.
elements.description: Instructed-response item; the original study excluded participants whose answer was not 3 (the paper does not give the wording).

elements.name: feel
elements.title: How does this image make you feel?
elements.description: 30 images per participant (15 positive, 15 negative, drawn at random, shown in random order). pleasantness: 1 = unpleasant, 5 = neutral, 9 = pleasant; activation: 1 = sleepy, 9 = awake (alert). key = image file name as in imageInfo on OSF wup5m (e.g. air_neg_img71).

elements.name: relevance
elements.title: How relevant do you think this image is to climate change?
elements.description: Asked on a second screen for the same image. 1 = not at all … 5 = very much. Same keys as feel.

elements.name: cc_belief
elements.title: Based on what you know, which of the following statements best describes your view on climate change? Choose one of the options.

choices.text: I believe the climate is not changing
I am not sure whether the climate is changing or not
I believe that the climate is changing, but that it has little to do with human conduct
I believe that the climate is changing, and that it is largely the result of human conduct

elements.name: risk
elements.title: Perceived risk of climate change (0 = no risk at all, 100 = extreme risk)
elements.description: { self, others, nonhuman } on 0–100 visual analogue scales; riskCC = mean of the three (risk1–risk3 in the open data).

elements.name: values

rows.text: ENJOYING LIFE: enjoying food, sex, leisure, etc.
SOCIAL POWER: control over others, dominance
AUTHORITY: the right to lead or command
INFLUENTIAL: having an impact on people and events
A WORLD AT PEACE: free of war and conflict
SOCIAL JUSTICE: correcting injustice, care for the weak
HELPFUL: working for the welfare of others
RESPECTING THE EARTH: harmony with other species
UNITY WITH NATURE: fitting into nature

elements.title: How important is each value as a guiding principle in your life?
elements.description: E-SVS (Steg et al., 2014), 16 values, −1 = against my principles, 0 = not important, 3 = important, 6 = very important, 7 = of supreme importance. hedonic = mean(hed1–hed3), egoistic = mean(ego1–ego5), altruistic = mean(alt1–alt4), biospheric = mean(bio1–bio4). Values are shown in random order.

config.description: Affective ratings of positive and negative environmental images for climate change research. Each participant rates 30 images drawn at random from the set (15 positive, 15 negative) in random order: how the image makes them feel (pleasantness 1–9, activation 1–9) and how relevant it is to climate change (1–5). Afterwards: belief in human-caused climate change, perceived risk of climate change to oneself, other people and non-human life (0–100), and the 16 environmental values of the E-SVS (−1 to 7). Rebuilt from Asutay (2026), Frontiers in Psychology, with the author's images from OSF wup5m.
